extracted.intended_audience: aspiring novelists, literary critics, and students of fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critical principles for writing and judging novels, with emphasis on subject, form, manner, and narrative method. Focused on how a novel's unity and the author's choices determine its artistic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read aright / get into touch with the book
rubrics_metrics.description: "The beginning of criticism is to read aright, in other words to get into touch with the book as nearly as may be."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism (and by implication the writer's self-critique) begins with an accurate, intimate apprehension of the work; there are degrees of unsuccess in failing to do this. One should judge the book's effect by first entering into its terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject unity should be concisely expressible
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is anyhow expressible in ten words that reveal its unity."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The novel's subject — whether a simple anecdote or an elaborate network of relationships — has an underlying unity that can be stated succinctly; recognising that unity is foundational to shaping the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form must be derived from the subject
rubrics_metrics.description: "The form of the book depends on it, and until it is known there is nothing to be said of the form."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choosing the book's form (structure, mode, presentation) should follow from the clarified subject; without knowing the subject's unity, decisions about form are premature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author's method should be integral and reveal imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: "his method will be a part of himself, and will tell us about the quality of his imagination."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The particular method or manner an author uses is an expression of the author's character and imaginative capacity; attention to manner (how the thing is done) is central to assessing craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide whether a character's account (narrator) is necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: "By all means let us have Harry's account if we must have somebody's, but perhaps there is no such need."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should judge the necessity of presenting events through a specific character's account or narration; include a narrated perspective only if it serves the work's unity and effect rather than from habit or convenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance dramatization and pictured impression; dramatization has limits
rubrics_metrics.description: "the art of dramatizing the picture of somebody's experience... touches its limit. There is indeed no further for it to go."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The technique of dramatizing experience can be pushed only so far before it reaches its limit; authors must choose between pushing toward dramatic enactment and moving toward a more pictorial, impressionistic presentation, understanding how that choice shifts the book's direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure characters are integrated into the single form of the book
rubrics_metrics.description: "Clarissa would have stepped out of the work of art ... the book would have perished. It is now a single form..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters must be handled so that they belong to and are sustained by the work's artistic form; elements that seem to 'step out' of the constructed form threaten the integrity and life of the book.
